PARENTING PLAN
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARENTS AND CHILD
This Parenting Plan is entered into by Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee ("the parents") regarding their child, Riley Lee. This Plan sets out the parents' agreement regarding legal custody, physical custody, and a visitation and timeshare schedule for Riley Lee, subject to the review and approval of a court with jurisdiction over this matter.

LEGAL AND PHYSICAL CUSTODY: JOINT AND SOLE, DEFINED
California law treats "custody" as two separate, independently-decided questions: legal custody (who has the right and responsibility to make decisions about a child's health, education, and welfare) and physical custody (with whom the child resides and who supervises the child day to day). Each question can be awarded jointly or solely, and the two axes can combine independently rather than as one all-or-nothing label. Joint legal custody means both Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee share the right and responsibility to make decisions relating to Riley Lee's health, education, and welfare. Sole legal custody means only one parent holds that right and responsibility. Joint physical custody means each parent has significant periods of physical custody, shared so as to assure Riley Lee of frequent and continuing contact with both parents. Sole physical custody means Riley Lee resides with and is supervised by one parent, subject to the court's power to order visitation for the other parent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "“Joint legal custody” means that both parents shall share the right and the responsibility to make the decisions relating to the health, education, and welfare of a child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3003 (California Legislative Information text), joint legal custody, defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3003.)
  "“Joint physical custody” means that each of the parents shall have significant periods of physical custody. Joint physical custody shall be shared by the parents in such a way so as to assure a child of frequent and continuing contact with both parents, subject to Sections 3011 and 3020."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3004 (California Legislative Information text), joint physical custody, defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3004.)
  "“Sole legal custody” means that one parent shall have the right and the responsibility to make the decisions relating to the health, education, and welfare of a child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3006 (California Legislative Information text), sole legal custody, defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3006.)
  "“Sole physical custody” means that a child shall reside with and be under the supervision of one parent, subject to the power of the court to order visitation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3007 (California Legislative Information text), sole physical custody, defined (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3007.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that legal custody and physical custody are two independently defined, independently awarded axes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Custody terminology and the joint/sole framework vary by state; some states use different labels (for example, "parenting time" rather than "physical custody") or a different default framework entirely. Each of the four definitions below comes from its own distinct Family Code section, not from subsections of a single section, so these four citations are independent of one another.

THE BEST-INTEREST-OF-THE-CHILD STANDARD AND ITS STATUTORY FACTORS
In making a custody determination, a California court is directed to consider — among any other factors it finds relevant — at least: the health, safety, and welfare of Riley Lee; any history of abuse by one parent or another person seeking custody against a child the person has cared for, against the other parent, or against certain other described household or relationship members; the nature and amount of Riley Lee's contact with both parents; and the habitual or continual illegal use of controlled substances, habitual or continual abuse of alcohol, or habitual or continual abuse of prescribed controlled substances by either parent. The court does not consider a parent's, legal guardian's, or relative's sex, gender identity, gender expression, or sexual orientation in this determination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) In making a determination of the best interests of the child in a proceeding described in Section 3021, the court shall, among any other factors it finds relevant and consistent with Section 3020, consider all of the following: (1) The health, safety, and welfare of the child. (2) (A) A history of abuse by one parent or any other person seeking custody against any of the following: (i) A child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom the parent or person seeking custody has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary. (ii) The other parent. (iii) A parent, current spouse, or cohabitant, of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom the parent or person seeking custody has a dating or engagement relationship."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a) (California Legislative Information text), the best-interest factors, part 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3011.)
  "(3) The nature and amount of contact with both parents, including as provided in Sections 3046 and 3100. (4) The habitual or continual illegal use of controlled substances, the habitual or continual abuse of alcohol, or the habitual or continual abuse of prescribed controlled substances by either parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(3)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), the best-interest factors, part 2 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3011.)
  "(b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the court shall not consider the sex, gender identity, gender expression, or sexual orientation of a parent, legal guardian, or relative in determining the best interests of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(b) (California Legislative Information text), the sex/gender/orientation exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3011.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific statutory best-interest factor list — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter, and not a claim that this list is exhaustive (the statute itself invites the court to weigh "any other factors it finds relevant"). Best-interest standards, and the specific factors a state's statute names, vary significantly by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3011); no additional independent source was found for this.

STATE POLICY: FREQUENT AND CONTINUING CONTACT, SUBJECT TO CHILD SAFETY
California's Family Code declares that the health, safety, and welfare of children is a court's primary concern in any custody or visitation order, and it is the state's public policy to ensure that Riley Lee has frequent and continuing contact with both Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee after separation — except when that contact would not be in Riley Lee's best interest. Where the safety-first policy and the frequent-contact policy point in different directions in a given case, the statute directs that the order be made in whatever manner ensures the health, safety, and welfare of the child and of all family members.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The Legislature finds and declares that it is the public policy of this state to ensure that the health, safety, and welfare of children shall be the court's primary concern in determining the best interests of children when making any orders regarding the physical or legal custody or visitation of children."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(a) (California Legislative Information text), child safety as the court's primary concern (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3020.)
  "The Legislature finds and declares that it is the public policy of this state to ensure that children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents after the parents have separated or dissolved their marriage, or ended their relationship, and to encourage parents to share the rights and responsibilities of child rearing in order to effect this policy, except when the contact would not be in the best interests of the child, as provided in subdivisions (a) and (c) of this section and Section 3011."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(b) (California Legislative Information text), the frequent-and-continuing-contact policy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3020.)
  "(c) When the policies set forth in subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section are in conflict, a court's order regarding physical or legal custody or visitation shall be made in a manner that ensures the health, safety, and welfare of the child and the safety of all family members."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3020(c) (California Legislative Information text), priority ordering when the two policies conflict (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3020.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, declared statutory priority ordering — child safety controls when it conflicts with the frequent-contact preference — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Whether, and how, a state's law states this kind of priority ordering between contact and safety varies by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3020); no additional independent source was found for this.

DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AND CUSTODY: THE REBUTTABLE PRESUMPTION
Under California law, a court finding that a parent seeking custody has perpetrated domestic violence within the preceding five years — against the other parent seeking custody, against Riley Lee or Riley Lee's siblings, or against certain other described persons connected to the parent — creates a rebuttable presumption that awarding that parent sole or joint physical or legal custody is detrimental to the child's best interest. The presumption can be rebutted only by a preponderance of the evidence, and the statute specifically states that the ordinary preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents may not, by itself, be used to rebut it. To overcome the presumption, the court must find the parent has demonstrated that custody is in the child's best interest, and must weigh additional factors including: completion of a batterer's treatment program meeting statutory criteria; completion of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, where the court finds it appropriate; completion of a parenting class, where the court finds it appropriate; the parent's probation or parole status and compliance; compliance with any protective or restraining order; whether the parent has committed further acts of domestic violence; and whether the court has found the parent to be a restrained person unlawfully in possession of a firearm or ammunition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child's siblings, or against a person in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011 with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child, pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. This presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(a) (California Legislative Information text), the rebuttable presumption itself (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  "(b) To overcome the presumption set forth in subdivision (a), the court shall find that paragraph (1) is satisfied and shall find that the factors in paragraph (2), on balance, support the legislative findings in Section 3020. (1) The perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. In determining the best interest of the child, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents, as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 3020, or with the noncustodial parent, as set forth in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part. (2) Additional factors: (A) The perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer's treatment program that meets the criteria outlined in subdivision (c) of Section 1203.097 of the Penal Code. (B) The perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines that counseling is appropriate. (C) The perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class to be appropriate. (D) The perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with the terms and conditions of probation or parole. (E) The perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions. (F) The perpetrator of domestic violence has committed further acts of domestic violence. (G) The court has determined, pursuant to Section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Section 6389, Section 527.9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Section 18120 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b) (California Legislative Information text), the factors for overcoming the presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3044.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, heavily litigated rebuttable presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter. Domestic-violence-related custody presumptions — including whether one exists at all, the look-back period, and the rebuttal factors — vary significantly by state. The version of this statute quoted here was enacted by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544 and became operative January 1, 2026; a document assembled from this text does not track future amendments to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3044); no additional independent source was found for this.

A PARENTS' CUSTODY AGREEMENT IS NOT SELF-EXECUTING
California law creates a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody serves a minor child's best interest where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a custody hearing — but that presumption is expressly made subject to the same best-interest factors the court otherwise applies. A parenting plan Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee reach between themselves is therefore evidence the court considers alongside the statutory best-interest factors, not an order in itself; it takes legal effect for Riley Lee only once incorporated into an order entered by a court with jurisdiction over the matter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "There is a presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that joint custody is in the best interest of a minor child, subject to Section 3011, where the parents have agreed to joint custody or so agree in open court at a hearing for the purpose of determining the custody of the minor child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3080 (California Legislative Information text), the joint-custody agreement presumption (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3080.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a parents' custody agreement functions as a rebuttable presumption feeding into the court's own best-interest determination, rather than as an automatically binding private contract — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. How strongly, and whether, a state's law defers to parents' own custody agreements varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 3080); no additional independent source was found for this.

Riley Lee's regular timeshare schedule with Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee is set out below:

☐ _________________________

Holiday, school-break, and other special-occasion schedules, where different from the regular schedule above, are set out separately below:

This schedule reflects only the parents' own description of their intended arrangement and does not state or imply any conclusion about what a court would order in a contested proceeding.

MODIFYING A CUSTODY ORDER: STATUTE AND UNWRITTEN DOCTRINE
A joint custody order can be modified or terminated on the petition of either or both parents, or on the court's own motion, if it is shown that Riley Lee's best interest requires the change; if either parent opposes the change, the statute requires the court to state its reasons for modifying or terminating the order.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An order for joint custody may be modified or terminated upon the petition of one or both parents or on the court's own motion if it is shown that the best interest of the child requires modification or termination of the order. If either parent opposes the modification or termination order, the court shall state in its decision the reasons for modification or termination of the joint custody order."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3087 (California Legislative Information text), modification or termination of a joint custody order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3087.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific standard governing modification or termination of a joint custody order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter. Beyond this joint-custody-termination provision, California's general changed-circumstances practice for modifying custody orders is judicial doctrine developed by California courts, not codified in one clean statute; this research did not independently verify a case citation for that doctrine through the primary-source, twice-fetched discipline used elsewhere in this document, so none is offered here rather than presenting an unverified citation as verified. This is a single statutory section (§ 3087); no additional independent source was found for this.

MEDIATION BEFORE A CONTESTED CUSTODY HEARING
Under California law, if it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading seeking to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court is required to set the contested issues for mediation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) If it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court shall set the contested issues for mediation."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(a) (California Legislative Information text), the mandatory mediation trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3170.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, mandatory pre-hearing mediation mechanism for contested custody or visitation matters — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody dispute. Whether mediation is required, optional, or unavailable, and on what trigger, varies substantially by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 3170(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

EQUAL ACCESS TO A CHILD'S RECORDS REGARDLESS OF CUSTODY
Under California law, access to records and information about Riley Lee — including, but not limited to, medical, dental, and school records — is not to be denied to Jordan Alex Lee or Morgan Casey Lee merely because that parent does not hold custody. This rule applies notwithstanding other provisions of law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, access to records and information pertaining to a minor child, including, but not limited to, medical, dental, and school records, shall not be denied to a parent because that parent is not the child's custodial parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3025 (California Legislative Information text), the records-access rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3025.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, self-executing records-access rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parenting plan or custody matter, and not a claim that no other statute or court order could ever limit this access. This research examined only the text of § 3025 itself and did not independently check for a separate statutory exception (for example, one tied to certain findings of abuse), so none is asserted here. This is a single statutory section (§ 3025); no additional independent source was found for this.

A CUSTODIAL PARENT'S PRESUMPTIVE RIGHT TO MOVE A CHILD'S RESIDENCE
In a different part of the Family Code than the custody chapter itself (Division 12, Parent and Child Relationship, rather than Division 8, Custody of Children), California law states that a parent entitled to custody of a child has a right to change the child's residence, subject to the power of the court to restrain a move that would prejudice the child's rights or welfare. The Legislature has stated its intent to affirm, and to declare as the public policy and law of the state, the California Supreme Court's decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) A parent entitled to the custody of a child has a right to change the residence of the child, subject to the power of the court to restrain a removal that would prejudice the rights or welfare of the child."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7501(a) (California Legislative Information text), the presumptive relocation right and the court's power to restrain it (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7501.)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature to affirm the decision in In re Marriage of Burgess (1996) 13 Cal.4th 25, and to declare that ruling to be the public policy and law of this state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 7501(b) (California Legislative Information text), the legislative intent to affirm In re Marriage of Burgess (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=7501.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific presumptive relocation right for a custodial parent, expressly subject to a court's power to restrain a prejudicial move — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific relocation or parenting-plan dispute. This provision sits in a different Division of the Family Code than the custody definitions and best-interest standard cited elsewhere in this document, and its interaction with a joint-custody or shared-timeshare arrangement — along with the substantial body of California case law interpreting Burgess since 1996 — is not independently verified or restated here. Relocation and "move-away" rules vary widely by state, and some states codify a move-away standard directly rather than through a general residence-change provision like this one. This is a single statutory section (§ 7501); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES
Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Morgan Casey Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This Parenting Plan becomes part of a court order only once reviewed and entered by a court with jurisdiction over Riley Lee's custody.
